title: Sounds, letters, and the first tricky words
title_target: Eu, é, jeung sababaraha kecap anu ngabobodo
goal: Get the *eu* sound right, tell *é* from *e*, and meet the first wave of words that sound familiar but mean something else.
bekal: say *eu* as one sound, not two
read *é* and *e* correctly even when the accent mark is missing
the ten tricky words that catch newcomers most often

dialogs.title: Paguneman — A slip of the tongue in the kitchen
dialogs.intro: Second evening. Rani is in the shared kitchen with her next-door neighbor at the boarding house, Néng Sari from Garut, who is frying something. (Rani is from Jakarta, so she speaks Indonesian — where *amis* means "fishy-smelling".)

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Téh Rani, hoyong nyobian? Ieu peuyeum.
lines.id: Rani, want to try some? This is peuyeum.
lines.literal: Téh Rani, want to-try? this peuyeum.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Peuyeum. Sakali baé, ulah dipisahkeun. Peuyeum.
lines.id: Peuyeum. All in one go, don't split it. Peuyeum.
lines.literal: peuyeum. once just, don't separated. peuyeum.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.id: Yes, that's right! So, is it amis?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Amis?! Ieu mah teu bau, Néng…
lines.id: Amis?! But it doesn't smell fishy, Néng…

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Hahaha! Amis dina basa Sunda téh manis, Téh. Lain bau lauk.
lines.id: Hahaha! In Sundanese, amis means sweet. Not fishy.
lines.literal: hahaha! amis in language Sundanese [téh] sweet, Téh. not smell fish.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Aduh. Kitu geuning. Manis pisan atuh ari kitu mah.
lines.id: Oh dear. So that's it. Then it's very sweet!
lines.literal: oh-dear. like-that it-turns-out. sweet very atuh if like-that [mah].

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Seueur kénéh nu kitu. Isukan Téh bakal manggih nu séjén.
lines.id: There are lots more like that. You'll run into others tomorrow.
lines.literal: many still which like-that. tomorrow Téh will find which other.

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Gering. Dina basa Sunda hartina gering téh nyeri, sanés begang.
lines.id: Gering. In Sundanese gering means sick, not skinny.
lines.literal: gering. in language Sundanese meaning-its gering [téh] sick, not skinny.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Untung teu acan kapopohokeun. Aya deui?
lines.id: Lucky I haven't used it wrong yet. Any more?
lines.literal: lucky not yet accidentally-used. there-is more?

lines.speaker: Sari:
lines.text: Aya. Tapi nu hiji mah engké waé, sieun Téteh éra.
lines.id: Yes. But that one can wait — you'd be embarrassed.
lines.literal: there-is. but which one [mah] later just, afraid Téteh embarrassed.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Ih, kade ah. Ayeuna waé atuh!
lines.id: Hey, watch it. Tell me now!
lines.literal: hey, careful ah. now just atuh!

notes: **Peuyeum** = fermented cassava, a Bandung specialty. The word is a good test because it contains **two** *eu* sounds in a row, and nearly every newcomer gets it wrong the first time. Say *peu-YEUM* in two beats, not *puh-oo-yuh-oom* in four.

**Amis** = sweet. ⚠️ This is the friendliest of the tricky words — the mistake is funny, not embarrassing. In Indonesian *amis* means "fishy-smelling"; in Sundanese it is praise for food. Other tastes: **pait** (bitter), **haseum** (sour), **asin** (salty), **peuheur** (astringent).
**Gering** = sick. ⚠️ Not "skinny", as in Indonesian. Skinny in Sundanese is **begang**. *Abdi gering* = I'm sick. The polite form for other people: *teu damang* or *udur*.

**Geuning** is a particle of surprise with no direct English equivalent. It means "it turns out", "oh, so…!", "well, look at that" — used when reality differs from what you expected. *Kitu geuning* = "oh, so that's how it is". *Aya geuning!* = "oh, there is one after all!" Note its position: always **after** the surprising thing.

**Mah** and **téh** appear four times in this dialogue and will appear in every unit from now on. For now, just get a feel for them: *ieu mah* = "as for this one", *amis téh* = "this word amis". Both are covered fully in Unit 8.
**Kade** = watch out, careful (loma). The full form is *kadé*, from *hadé* (good) — literally "nicely, now". It is often used half-jokingly, as in this dialogue.

**Éra** = embarrassed, ashamed. You will hear it often in talk about manners, because a sense of shame is one of the guardians of Sundanese politeness. *Éra ku sorangan* = ashamed in front of yourself.

grammars.title: The é mark that often disappears, and how to guess it
body: This course always writes *é* with its accent mark. The world outside the course doesn't. Signboards, food-stall menus, WhatsApp messages, and most books write every *e* without the mark — and readers guess from which word makes sense.
You can guess too, because the guess isn't random. These three patterns cover most cases:

head: Pattern
Examples
Sound
rows: Words borrowed from Indonesian keep their weak *e*
Native Sundanese words ending in *-eun*, *-euh*, *-eur* use **eu**, not e
Most native Sundanese words with *-é-* in the middle use the clear **é**

after: When in doubt, listen to someone say the word once, then file it away. Sundanese doesn't have many word pairs told apart only by *é* and *e*, so a wrong guess rarely causes a misunderstanding — it just makes you sound like a reader, not a speaker.

⚠️ One exception worth memorizing because it comes up a lot: **entéh** (tea, the drink) has the clear *é* in the second syllable, while **énték** (used up, finished) has it in the first. Mix them up and *entéh* sounds like *énték*, and your order at the food stall turns comic.

grammars.title: Ten tricky words — first wave
body: The words below sound familiar to anyone who has picked up some Indonesian — the language of shops, signs, and TV all over West Java — and that is exactly why they are dangerous. Learn them now; more follow in later units, and the full list is at the back of the book.
after: ⚠️ Read the last one twice. In Indonesian, *bujur* means "true" — and people from Jakarta checking a fact sometimes say "bujur, kan?" ("right?"). In Sundanese, *bujur* means **buttocks**. The word you want is **leres** (right, true — lemes) or **enya/bener** (loma).

**Atos** has two meanings, told apart by context: as a helper verb it means "already" (*atos didahar* = already eaten); as an adjective it means "hard" (*rotina atos* = the bread is hard). The more polite word for "already" is **parantos**, and the loma form is **geus**.

blocks.text: The *eu* sound appears in hundreds of everyday words, so it isn't a decoration you can skip. Here is a practice ladder, from easiest to hardest. Say each line five times until it feels like one beat.

blocks.title: Test sentences
items: **Seueur teuing, euy!** — Way too much, man! (*euy* = a friendly Sundanese exclamation)
**Euweuh nanaon.** — There's nothing. / It's nothing.
**Bajuna beureum, calanana hideung.** — The shirt is red, the trousers are black.
**Ulah heureuy waé atuh.** — Come on, stop joking around all the time.
**Aya inumeun teu?** — Is there anything to drink?

sections.title: Letters that aren't native to Sundanese

blocks.text: Four letters never appear in native Sundanese words: **f, v, z, sy** (the *sh* sound). They all came in through loanwords, and older speakers replace them with the nearest native sound. You don't have to copy this — but you do need to recognize it, because words like *telepisi* or *sukur* will look misspelled when they are in fact the forms people use.
The standard Sundanese script later added special letters for *fa*, *va*, *za*, *qa*, and *xa* so that names and loanwords could be written — you will see them for yourself in Unit 19.

This is the quickest accent fix there is, and it is almost never taught. English speakers (and Indonesian speakers) tend to stress an earlier syllable: *I-mah*, *DA-har*. Sundanese stresses the **last** syllable, so sentences sound as if they rise at the end.

The exception: words with the suffixes *-eun*, *-keun*, *-na*, and *-an* pull the stress to the syllable before the suffix, so *daharaneun* is said *dah-hah-rah-NEUN* but *dibawakeun* is said *dee-bah-WAH-keun*. You don't need to memorize this; it comes by itself with plenty of listening.

blocks.title: The most useful five-minute drill
items: Take the Unit 1 dialogue and read it aloud once with English-style stress.
Read it again stressing the last syllable of **every** word, exaggerated until it sounds over the top.
Read it a third time halfway between the two. That is roughly the right sound.
Repeat daily for a week with the dialogue of whichever unit you are on.

answers: seu-eur — hi-deung — heu-reuy — beu-reum — eu-weuh — i-nu-meun
sweet — sick — child — buttocks — please, go ahead — fish
Punten, leres ieu jalan ka Dago? — Adi kuring begang, awakna alit pisan. — Ieu entéhna amis pisan, ngeunah. — This sentence is already correct: "budak" means child. — Sok atuh, ulah kitu ka kolot.
Euweuh nanaon. — Bajuna beureum, calanana hideung. — Seueur teuing, euy! — Aya inumeun teu? — Ulah heureuy waé atuh. — Kitu geuning.
